explanations.explanation: Day and night. Heman never clocks out. He says, "O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You." I think that tells you how heavy things are for him. He's hurting and he's still talking to God.

Once a year is how often I clean behind my oven, and I'm not proud of it. Heman is on a very different schedule. He says, "…day and night I cry out before You." That's not a yearly visit. That's day and night.
Heman doesn't wait for a special day. The psalm says, "…day and night I cry out before You." That covers the plain old Tuesdays too. Nothing in this verse ties his crying to a calendar.
Ear. Heman asks, "incline Your ear to my cry." It's the picture of someone leaning in close to listen. I think he mostly wants to be heard right now. Most of us know that feeling.

A hand would make sense if he were asking for a rescue, but that's not the request here. He asks the LORD to "incline Your ear to my cry." It's a listening request. I think a person this worn out first wants to be heard.
A staff is a great picture, but it isn't in this verse. Heman asks the LORD to "incline Your ear to my cry." He's asking to be heard.

Those descending to the Pit. He says, "I am counted among those descending to the Pit." That's his way of saying he feels close to the end. Then he adds, "I am like a man without strength." I think he's tired all the way down.

David, Israel's king, had a famous group of mighty men (2 Samuel 23:8). They aren't in this psalm, though. Heman says the opposite of strong: "I am like a man without strength." He says, "I am counted among those descending to the Pit."

explanations.answer: The elders at the city gate
explanations.explanation: Sitting with the elders sounds like a spot of respect, and Heman isn't claiming one. He says, "I am counted among those descending to the Pit." That's about as far from a seat of honor as you can get. He's describing how low he feels.

True. He calls them ones "…whom You remember no more, who are cut off from Your care." That's how he describes them. This is one of the heavy lines, so let's let it sit a moment. I think it hurts to read, and it's okay to feel that.

The text says the opposite. Heman describes the slain as ones "…whom You remember no more, who are cut off from Your care." He says he's forsaken among the dead, like them. I think this is one of the heaviest lines in the psalm.
True. He tells the LORD, "You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths." He says it straight to God, not behind His back. I think that's honest praying. He doesn't dress it up.

The text says it is the LORD. Heman tells Him, "You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths." Notice he says it right to the LORD's face. I think that's what honest prayer looks like.
Waves. He says, "all Your waves have submerged me." Picture trying to come up for air and another one rolls in. It's a water picture, not a battlefield. Heman feels buried under it.
Armies would be loud and dramatic, and I do love loud. But the verse picks water. Heman says, "all Your waves have submerged me." It's a sea picture, not a battle one.
Clouds drift by softly, and nothing here is soft. Heman says, "all Your waves have submerged me." He's under the water, not under a sky.

Repulsive. He says, "You have made me repulsive to them…" It's a strong word, and it means he's pushed away from the friends he had. I think the loneliness here weighs as much as the Pit. That's a lot for one person to carry.

Precious is what you'd hope for, but the verse says the opposite. Heman says the LORD has made him "…repulsive to them…" His friends are gone, and that's how he describes where he stands with them. I think that makes everything lonelier.
Useful sounds like a line on a work review. The verse uses a much sadder word. Heman says the LORD has made him "…repulsive to them…"

The text says the opposite. Heman says, "I am confined and cannot escape." No secret door and no loose board. I think he feels stuck in the dark with nowhere to go. I know a little about that feeling from the back of a junk drawer.

False. Heman says, "I am confined and cannot escape." He doesn't mention any way out at all. I know a little about feeling stuck in the dark, from my years in the back of a junk drawer. I think he's feeling it far deeper than I ever did.

explanations.answer: Spreads them out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: He says, "I spread out my hands to You." His eyes grow dim with grief, and he still calls to the LORD daily. That's the part I'd tell a friend about.

Covering your face is a very human thing to do when things hurt, but it isn't in this verse. Heman says, "I spread out my hands to You." Open hands, reaching toward the LORD. I think that takes more than I'd manage on a hard day.
Tearing clothes shows up elsewhere in the Bible. Jacob, Joseph's father, tore his clothes in his grief (Genesis 37:34). But that's not what Heman does here. He says, "I spread out my hands to You."

Angels aren't in the question at all. Heman asks, "Do You work wonders for the dead?" It's about wonders, and about the dead. I think he's wondering what becomes of praise when a person is gone. That's a heavy thing to ask.
False. His first question is, "Do You work wonders for the dead?" No angels, just wonders. He puts it right to the LORD.

Grave. He asks, "Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?" The questions keep stacking up, one right after the other. He doesn't hold them back. He puts them right to the LORD.

The heavens are where you'd expect devotion to be sung, but the question goes lower. Heman asks, "Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?" It's a question about the grave. I think he's looking at the darkest place he can think of.

A city is where people gather and talk, so I see why you'd guess it. But Heman is asking about a quieter place. He says, "Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?" The word is grave.

explanations.answer: Cries to the LORD for help
explanations.explanation: He says, "But to You, O LORD, I cry for help; in the morning my prayer comes before You." After all those questions, he turns right back to the LORD. That little word "But" is doing a lot of work. I love that he keeps going.

explanations.answer: Waits in silence before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Silence before the LORD is a good thing, but it's not what this verse says. Heman says, "But to You, O LORD, I cry for help…" He isn't quiet. He cries out, and he keeps on asking.

explanations.answer: Sings a song of thanks to the LORD
explanations.explanation: A song of thanks would be a nice turn, but it isn't here. Heman says, "But to You, O LORD, I cry for help…" He's still asking. I think that's honest, because he doesn't pretend to feel better than he does.
Face. He asks, "Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?" Two questions, right to the LORD. I think those are hard questions to ask.
Law is a big Bible word, but it isn't in this verse. Heman asks, "Why do You hide Your face from me?" It's about the LORD's face. I think it's a lonely question to ask.
Name is an important word in Scripture, but this verse is about something else. Heman asks, "Why do You hide Your face from me?" The word is face. I think it's a lonely thing to ask the LORD.
He says, "From my youth I was afflicted and near death." That's not a rough week, that's a long road. I think that's why he sounds so tired. He's been carrying this a very long time.
Seven years is a number the verse never gives. Heman says, "From my youth I was afflicted and near death." He points back to when he was young. I think it's been a long road.

Forty days shows up in other Bible stories, like the rain in Noah's day. Noah built the ark, and the rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights (Genesis 7:12). But Heman gives a different answer. He says, "From my youth I was afflicted and near death."
True. He says, "All day long they engulf me like water…" It's not just a moment, it's all day. I think that's the tiring part. There's no stretch where it lets up.
The text says the opposite. Heman says, "All day long they engulf me like water…" Not once, not for an hour, but all day long. I think that's part of why he's so worn out.
On every side. He says, "they enclose me on every side." There's no gap to slip through. It lines up with what he said earlier: "I am confined and cannot escape."
Only from above would leave room to run sideways. But Heman says, "they enclose me on every side." Every side means no gap. That's the whole point of the picture.
From behind alone would leave a way forward. But Heman says, "they enclose me on every side." That means all around him. I think that's why he feels so trapped.

Darkness. His last line is, "darkness is my closest companion." His beloved and his friend are gone, and the dark is what's left. It's a heavy way to end. Still, the whole psalm is spoken to the LORD.

A harp would be a gentle friend, but the psalm never mentions one. The last line says, "darkness is my closest companion." That's the final word. I think it's one of the heaviest endings in the Bible.

The morning does show up earlier, in verse 13: "in the morning my prayer comes before You." But the very last line is different. It says, "darkness is my closest companion." The morning is where he prays, not where he ends.
The psalm ends the other way. Heman's last line is, "darkness is my closest companion." There's no burst of praise to close it out. I think it's a heavy ending, and it's okay to say so.

False. The final line is, "darkness is my closest companion." It's a quiet, heavy ending, with nothing tied up in a bow. I think there's something honest about that. Heman brought all of it to the LORD.
